cards: Cell-surface membrane, nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi apparatus and vesicles, lysosomes, ribosomes, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum. Plant cells also have a cellulose cell wall, chloroplasts and a vacuole.
Contains chromosomes (DNA with histones) and a nucleolus that makes ribosomes. The nuclear envelope has pores that let mRNA leave.
Site of aerobic respiration, producing ATP. Double membrane with the inner membrane folded into cristae; the matrix contains enzymes.
Site of photosynthesis. Contain thylakoids stacked into grana (light-dependent reaction) surrounded by the stroma (light-independent reaction).
Rough ER has ribosomes and synthesises and transports proteins. The Golgi apparatus modifies and packages proteins and lipids into vesicles and makes lysosomes.
Vesicles containing hydrolytic enzymes (lysozymes) that digest pathogens and break down old organelles.
No nucleus or membrane-bound organelles; circular DNA not associated with histones; smaller 70S ribosomes; murein cell wall. May have plasmids, a capsule and flagella.
Acellular and non-living. Genetic material and enzymes such as reverse transcriptase inside a capsid, with attachment proteins. Some have a lipid envelope.
Magnification = size of image ÷ size of real object. Remember 1 mm = 1000 µm.
The minimum distance apart two objects can be and still be seen as separate. Electron microscopes have higher resolution because electrons have a shorter wavelength than light.

Transmission EM gives 2D images with very high resolution of internal structures; specimens must be very thin. Scanning EM gives 3D surface images at lower resolution. Both need a vacuum, so specimens are dead.
Homogenise cells in cold, isotonic, buffered solution, filter, then ultracentrifuge at increasing speeds. Nuclei sediment first, then mitochondria, then lysosomes/ER, then ribosomes.
Why the solution is cold, isotonic and buffered
Cold reduces enzyme activity that would digest organelles; isotonic prevents osmosis damaging organelles; buffered prevents pH changes denaturing proteins.
A network of protein fibres (microfilaments, microtubules) that supports the cell, moves organelles and enables cell movement.
Made of microtubules; involved in forming the spindle during cell division.
Hair-like extensions made of microtubules in a 9+2 arrangement, used for movement of the cell or of fluid past it.
Differential staining (e.g. Gram staining, methylene blue) increases contrast so structures can be seen.
Uses a laser to scan a specimen at set depths, producing clear, high-resolution images, often of fluorescent-tagged structures.
The eyepiece graticule is calibrated against a stage micrometer at each magnification to measure specimens.
Monomers are small units that join to form larger molecules called polymers. Examples of monomers: monosaccharides, amino acids and nucleotides.
A condensation reaction joins two molecules with a chemical bond and removes a molecule of water. A hydrolysis reaction breaks a chemical bond between two molecules using a molecule of water.
Glucose, galactose and fructose. Glucose has two isomers, α-glucose and β-glucose, which differ in the position of the OH group on carbon 1.
Maltose = glucose + glucose. Sucrose = glucose + fructose. Lactose = glucose + galactose. Each is formed by a condensation reaction that makes a glycosidic bond.
Both are polymers of α-glucose. Starch (amylose and amylopectin) is the plant store; glycogen is the animal store and is more highly branched, so it can be hydrolysed quickly to release glucose.
Why starch and glycogen are good stores
Insoluble, so they don't affect water potential; large, so they can't leave the cell; compact; branching gives many ends for rapid hydrolysis by enzymes.
A polymer of β-glucose. Alternate monomers are inverted, giving long straight chains held together by many hydrogen bonds to form microfibrils, which give plant cell walls strength.
Add Benedict's reagent and heat in a water bath. A positive result goes from blue to green, yellow, orange or brick-red precipitate.

After a negative Benedict's test, boil the sample with dilute hydrochloric acid, neutralise with sodium hydrogencarbonate, then repeat the Benedict's test. A coloured precipitate shows a non-reducing sugar such as sucrose.
Add iodine/potassium iodide solution. A colour change from orange-brown to blue-black shows starch is present.
One glycerol and three fatty acids joined by ester bonds formed in condensation reactions. Saturated fatty acids have no C=C double bonds; unsaturated ones have at least one.
High ratio of C-H bonds so they release lots of energy; low mass for energy stored; insoluble so don't affect water potential; release metabolic water when oxidised.
One fatty acid of a triglyceride is replaced by a phosphate-containing group. The phosphate head is hydrophilic and the fatty acid tails are hydrophobic, so they form a bilayer in membranes.
Mix the sample with ethanol, then add water and shake. A milky-white emulsion shows lipid is present.
A central carbon attached to an amine group (NH2), a carboxyl group (COOH), a hydrogen atom and a variable R group. There are 20 amino acids common to all organisms.
Formed by a condensation reaction between the amine group of one amino acid and the carboxyl group of another. Many amino acids join to form a polypeptide.
The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide chain. It determines how the protein folds and so its final shape and function.
Hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N-H groups of the backbone fold the chain into an α-helix or β-pleated sheet.
Further folding into a specific 3D shape held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and disulfide bridges between R groups.
More than one polypeptide chain joined together, sometimes with a prosthetic group (e.g. haemoglobin has four chains and haem groups).
Add biuret reagent (sodium hydroxide and copper(II) sulfate). A colour change from blue to purple shows protein is present.
Enzymes are biological catalysts that lower the activation energy of reactions. The substrate binds to the active site to form an enzyme-substrate complex.
The active site is not exactly complementary at first; it changes shape slightly as the substrate binds, putting strain on bonds and lowering activation energy.
Rate rises with temperature as kinetic energy increases collisions. Above the optimum, hydrogen and ionic bonds break, the active site changes shape and the enzyme is denatured.
Changes in pH alter the charges on R groups in the active site, breaking ionic and hydrogen bonds, so the active site changes shape and fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form.
The inhibitor has a similar shape to the substrate and binds to the active site. Increasing substrate concentration reduces its effect.
The inhibitor binds to a site other than the active site (allosteric site), changing the shape of the active site. Increasing substrate concentration does not reduce its effect.
Rate increases as more enzyme-substrate complexes form, until all active sites are occupied and the rate levels off; enzyme concentration then becomes the limiting factor.
Fibrous proteins (collagen, keratin, elastin) are insoluble and structural. Globular proteins (haemoglobin, insulin, pepsin) are soluble with specific shapes for metabolic roles.
A fibrous protein of three polypeptide chains wound together, with many cross-links, giving high tensile strength in tendons, skin and bones.
Colorimetry measures colour intensity, e.g. of Benedict's solution after a test, to estimate concentration using a calibration curve. Biosensors can also be used.
Separates biological molecules such as amino acids; Rf value = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent.
A pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogen-containing organic base. In DNA the sugar is deoxyribose; in RNA it is ribose.
Adenine pairs with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and cytosine pairs with guanine (three hydrogen bonds). In RNA, uracil replaces thymine.
Formed by a condensation reaction between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the sugar of another, forming the sugar-phosphate backbone.
Two antiparallel polynucleotide strands held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases, twisted into a double helix.
How DNA's structure suits its function
Stable sugar-phosphate backbone; hydrogen bonds allow strands to separate for replication; complementary base pairing allows accurate copying; very long, so stores lots of information.

DNA helicase breaks hydrogen bonds to unwind the strands. Free nucleotides pair with exposed complementary bases. DNA polymerase joins adjacent nucleotides with phosphodiester bonds. Each new molecule has one original and one new strand.
Grew bacteria in heavy nitrogen (15N) then light nitrogen (14N). After one generation all DNA had intermediate density, supporting semi-conservative replication.
A nucleotide derivative of adenine with ribose and three phosphate groups.
ATP hydrolase hydrolyses ATP to ADP and inorganic phosphate, releasing a small, manageable amount of energy. The phosphate can phosphorylate other compounds, making them more reactive.
ATP synthase joins ADP and Pi in a condensation reaction during photosynthesis and respiration.

Metabolite in condensation and hydrolysis; important solvent; high specific heat capacity buffers temperature changes; large latent heat of vaporisation gives cooling by evaporation; cohesion supports water columns and surface tension.
Hydrogen ions affect pH; iron ions are part of haemoglobin; sodium ions are used in co-transport of glucose and amino acids; phosphate ions are part of DNA, RNA and ATP.
Phosphorylated nucleotides; ATP releases energy when hydrolysed to ADP and Pi.
Purines (adenine and guanine) have two rings; pyrimidines (cytosine, thymine, uracil) have one. A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine.
Grind tissue with detergent and salt, add protease, then layer ice-cold ethanol so DNA precipitates out.
Cofactors are non-protein substances needed for enzyme activity (e.g. Cl⁻ for amylase). Coenzymes are organic cofactors, often from vitamins. Prosthetic groups are permanently bound.
The product of a metabolic pathway inhibits an earlier enzyme, regulating the pathway by negative feedback.
Q10 = rate at (T + 10 °C) ÷ rate at T. For enzyme-controlled reactions it is about 2 below the optimum.
Catalase works inside cells; amylase and trypsin work outside cells.
Some enzymes are produced inactive (e.g. pepsinogen) to prevent damage to cells, then activated where needed.
Rate increases with enzyme concentration if substrate is in excess.
Many act as enzyme inhibitors, e.g. cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase; penicillin inhibits enzymes making bacterial cell walls.
Phospholipid bilayer with proteins, glycoproteins, glycolipids and cholesterol. Fluid because phospholipids move; mosaic because proteins are scattered through it.
Binds to phospholipid tails, restricting their movement, which makes the membrane less fluid and more rigid.
Net movement of molecules from high to low concentration, passive. Small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse across the bilayer.
Passive movement of larger or charged molecules down a concentration gradient through channel proteins or carrier proteins.
Net movement of water from an area of higher water potential to lower water potential across a partially permeable membrane. Pure water has a water potential of 0 kPa.
Movement against a concentration gradient using carrier proteins and energy from the hydrolysis of ATP.

Sodium ions are actively pumped out of epithelial cells into the blood. Sodium then diffuses into the cell from the lumen with glucose via a co-transporter protein; glucose then moves into the blood by facilitated diffusion.
Surface area, concentration gradient, thickness of exchange surface, and number of channel or carrier proteins.
Microvilli increase surface area; many mitochondria supply ATP for active transport; many carrier proteins.
Effect of temperature on membrane permeability (beetroot)
Higher temperature increases phospholipid movement and denatures proteins, so the membrane becomes more permeable and more pigment leaks out.
Bulk transport using vesicles and ATP: endocytosis takes substances in; exocytosis releases substances out of the cell.
In a hypotonic solution plant cells become turgid; in a hypertonic solution they lose water and become plasmolysed.
Animal cells burst (haemolysis) in pure water and shrink (crenate) in concentrated solutions.
Glycoproteins and glycolipids on membranes act as receptors and antigens, allowing cell recognition and communication.
Interphase (DNA replication and organelle synthesis), mitosis (nuclear division) and cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm).
Chromosomes condense and become visible; the nuclear envelope breaks down; spindle fibres form from centrioles.
Chromosomes line up along the equator of the cell, attached to spindle fibres by their centromeres.
Centromeres divide and spindle fibres shorten, pulling sister chromatids to opposite poles.
Chromatids reach the poles and become chromosomes again; nuclear envelopes reform, producing two genetically identical nuclei.
Number of cells with visible chromosomes ÷ total number of cells observed. Shows the proportion of cells dividing.
Stain with toluidine blue or acetic orcein, warm with hydrochloric acid to separate cells, squash gently and view under a light microscope.
Cancer results from uncontrolled cell division forming a tumour. Many treatments target the cell cycle, for example by stopping DNA replication or spindle formation.
How prokaryotes divide: replication of the circular DNA and plasmids, then division of the cytoplasm to produce two daughter cells.
Viruses do not divide. They inject nucleic acid into a host cell, and the host's machinery replicates the virus particles.
A change in the base sequence of DNA, such as a substitution or deletion. A deletion causes a frameshift. Due to the degenerate code, not all substitutions change the amino acid.
Factors that increase the rate of mutation, such as ionising radiation, UV light and some chemicals.
Non-disjunction (chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis) changes the number of chromosomes, for example polyploidy or Down's syndrome.
Two divisions produce four genetically different haploid cells. Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II separates chromatids.
Homologous chromosomes pair up and chromatids twist around each other, exchanging sections of DNA at chiasmata, creating new combinations of alleles.
Homologous pairs line up randomly in meiosis I, so each gamete gets a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes.
Independent segregation gives 2ⁿ possible combinations, where n is the number of homologous pairs. Random fertilisation increases variation further.
Mitosis: one division, two genetically identical diploid cells. Meiosis: two divisions, four genetically varied haploid cells.
G1, G2 and spindle assembly checkpoints check for DNA damage and correct replication before division continues.
Erythrocytes (no nucleus, biconcave), neutrophils (lobed nucleus, many lysosomes), sperm, palisade cells, root hair cells and guard cells.
Squamous and ciliated epithelia, cartilage and muscle.
Stem cells divide and differentiate. Uses: treating heart disease, type 1 diabetes, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and repairing nervous tissue. Bone marrow and meristems contain stem cells.
Plant stem cells in the cambium give rise to xylem and phloem.
Larger organisms have a smaller SA:V ratio, so they need specialised exchange surfaces and mass transport systems. Small organisms can rely on diffusion across their surface.
Rate of diffusion is proportional to surface area × concentration difference ÷ thickness of the exchange surface.
Air enters through spiracles into tracheae and tracheoles, which reach every cell. Ventilation by abdominal pumping; water in tracheole ends is drawn out during exercise, increasing surface area.
Waterproof waxy cuticle, small surface area to volume ratio, and spiracles that can close.
Gills have filaments covered in lamellae for a large surface area. Countercurrent flow keeps a concentration gradient along the whole length of the lamellae.
Blood and water flow in opposite directions, so the water always has a higher oxygen concentration than the blood it meets, and diffusion happens across the whole lamella.
Gases diffuse through stomata into air spaces of the spongy mesophyll. Guard cells close stomata to reduce water loss.
Plants adapted to dry conditions: thick waxy cuticle, sunken stomata, hairs, rolled leaves and fewer stomata, all trapping moist air and reducing water potential gradient.
Trachea, bronchi, bronchioles and alveoli. Alveoli have a thin epithelium (one cell thick) and a large surface area, surrounded by capillaries.
External intercostal muscles contract and internal relax, so the ribcage moves up and out; the diaphragm contracts and flattens; thoracic volume increases, pressure decreases and air moves in.
Mostly passive: external intercostals and diaphragm relax, volume decreases, pressure increases and air is forced out. Forced expiration uses the internal intercostal muscles.
Tidal volume × ventilation rate (breaths per minute).
Correlation between risk factors (e.g. smoking, pollution) and disease does not prove causation. Fibrosis, asthma and emphysema reduce gas exchange or ventilation.
Cartilage keeps airways open; ciliated epithelium and goblet cells trap and move mucus; smooth muscle and elastic fibres control airway size.
Measures vital capacity, tidal volume, breathing rate and oxygen uptake. Soda lime absorbs CO2.
The maximum volume of air that can be breathed out after a maximum breath in.
The mouth and opercula create pressure changes that keep water flowing over the gills in one direction.
A protein with quaternary structure: four polypeptide chains each with a haem group containing iron, so each molecule carries four oxygen molecules.

S-shaped. Binding of the first oxygen changes the shape of haemoglobin, making it easier for others to bind (cooperative binding). High affinity at high partial pressure in the lungs; unloads at low partial pressure in tissues.
Higher carbon dioxide concentration lowers the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen, shifting the curve to the right, so more oxygen is unloaded to respiring tissues.
Animals in low-oxygen environments have haemoglobin with higher affinity (curve shifted left). Small, active animals have lower affinity (curve shifted right) to unload more oxygen.
Blood passes through the heart twice per circuit: pulmonary circulation to the lungs and systemic circulation to the body. Keeps pressure high for efficient delivery.
Coronary arteries supply the heart; pulmonary artery and vein; aorta and vena cava; renal arteries and veins.
Atrial systole (atria contract, AV valves open), ventricular systole (ventricles contract, AV valves close, semilunar valves open), then diastole (heart relaxes and fills).

Open when pressure behind them is higher and close when pressure in front is higher, preventing backflow. AV valves are between atria and ventricles; semilunar valves are in the aorta and pulmonary artery.
Arteries: thick muscular and elastic walls for high pressure. Arterioles: muscle constricts to control flow. Capillaries: one cell thick for exchange. Veins: wide lumen, thin walls and valves.

At the arteriole end, high hydrostatic pressure forces fluid out of capillaries. At the venule end, lower water potential in the capillary (due to plasma proteins) draws water back by osmosis. Excess drains into the lymph.
Smoking, high blood pressure, high blood cholesterol, obesity, lack of exercise and genetics. Atheroma formation can lead to aneurysm and myocardial infarction.
Single, double, open and closed circulatory systems
Fish have a single closed system; mammals a double closed system; insects have an open system where haemolymph bathes organs.
Records the heart's electrical activity. Abnormalities include tachycardia, bradycardia, ectopic heartbeat and atrial fibrillation.
As hydrogencarbonate ions leave red blood cells, chloride ions move in to keep the charge balanced.
About 85% as hydrogencarbonate ions (carbonic anhydrase), some as carbaminohaemoglobin and some dissolved in plasma.
Has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin, so it takes oxygen from the mother's blood in the placenta.
Water evaporates from leaves (transpiration), creating tension that pulls water up the xylem. Hydrogen bonds make water molecules cohesive, forming a continuous column; adhesion to xylem walls helps.
Tree trunk diameter is smaller during the day when tension is highest; if xylem is broken, air is drawn in and water no longer leaks out.
Measures water uptake, used to estimate transpiration rate. Cut shoot under water, ensure airtight seal, and time the movement of an air bubble.
Light intensity (more stomata open), temperature, humidity and wind speed.
Movement of assimilates such as sucrose in the phloem from sources (e.g. leaves) to sinks (e.g. roots, growing tissues), using energy.

Sucrose is actively loaded into sieve tubes at the source, lowering water potential so water enters by osmosis, raising pressure. At the sink sucrose is removed, so water leaves, and the pressure gradient pushes sap from source to sink.
Ringing experiments (bulge above the ring), tracer experiments with radioactive carbon, and aphid mouthparts showing sap under pressure.
Xylem: dead, hollow, lignified vessels for water and minerals. Phloem: living sieve tube elements with sieve plates, supported by companion cells.
Symplast (through cytoplasm and plasmodesmata) and apoplast (through cell walls) pathways. The Casparian strip forces water into the symplast at the endodermis.
Active pumping of minerals into the xylem lowers water potential, so water moves in by osmosis and is pushed up.
Plants adapted to water, e.g. water lilies have air spaces (aerenchyma) and stomata on the upper surface.
A molecule (usually a protein) on the surface of a cell that generates an immune response. Lets the immune system identify pathogens, abnormal body cells, toxins and cells from other organisms.
A phagocyte engulfs a pathogen into a phagosome. A lysosome fuses with it and hydrolytic enzymes destroy the pathogen. The phagocyte then presents the antigens.
Helper T cells with complementary receptors bind to antigens on antigen-presenting cells. They stimulate cytotoxic T cells (which kill infected cells using perforin), B cells and phagocytes.
A B cell with a complementary antibody binds the antigen, takes it in and presents it. Helper T cells activate it, and it divides by mitosis (clonal selection) into plasma cells and memory cells.
Four polypeptide chains (two heavy, two light) with variable regions forming two antigen-binding sites, and a constant region.
They bind to complementary antigens forming antigen-antibody complexes, causing agglutination so phagocytes can engulf many pathogens at once.
Primary response is slow with few antibodies, so symptoms appear. Memory cells make the secondary response faster and stronger, so the pathogen is destroyed before symptoms.

Active: the body makes its own antibodies after exposure or vaccination, and is long-term. Passive: antibodies are given (e.g. via placenta or breast milk); it is immediate but short-term with no memory cells.
Vaccines contain antigens that trigger memory cell production. Herd immunity: if enough people are vaccinated, the pathogen can't spread easily, protecting unvaccinated people.
When pathogens change their antigens (e.g. influenza), memory cells no longer recognise them, so new vaccines are needed.
HIV has RNA, reverse transcriptase and attachment proteins in a capsid with a lipid envelope. It infects helper T cells, and reverse transcriptase makes DNA from its RNA, which joins the host DNA.
HIV kills helper T cells, so the immune system can't stimulate B cells or cytotoxic T cells, leaving the person vulnerable to opportunistic infections.
Why antibiotics don't work on viruses
Antibiotics target bacterial structures such as murein cell walls and 70S ribosomes. Viruses have no cell wall and use host cell ribosomes.

Monoclonal antibodies come from a single clone of plasma cells. They're used for targeted drug delivery, pregnancy tests and the ELISA test, which uses an enzyme-linked antibody to detect an antigen by a colour change.
Bacteria (tuberculosis, bacterial meningitis, ring rot), viruses (HIV/AIDS, influenza, TMV), protoctista (malaria, potato blight) and fungi (black sigatoka, ringworm, athlete's foot).
Direct (contact, inoculation, ingestion) and indirect (fomites, droplets, vectors such as mosquitoes for malaria).
Passive: cellulose cell walls, waxy cuticle, bark, stomatal closure. Active: callose deposition, chemical defences such as tannins, and necrosis.
Skin, mucous membranes, blood clotting, inflammation, wound repair and expulsive reflexes.
Proteins that bind to pathogens and make them easier for phagocytes to engulf.
Overuse allows resistant bacteria to survive and multiply, e.g. MRSA and C. difficile.
Many drugs come from plants and microorganisms (e.g. penicillin), so biodiversity must be protected. Personalised medicine and synthetic biology create new drugs.
A group of organisms that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
Allows recognition of members of the same species and of a mate capable of breeding; species-specific behaviour.
Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Groups are nested with no overlap.
The genus and species name, e.g. Homo sapiens. Genus has a capital letter; both are written in italics or underlined.
Species richness is the number of different species in a community. The index of diversity also considers how many individuals of each species there are.
d = N(N-1) ÷ Σn(n-1), where N is total number of organisms and n is the number of each species. Higher values mean greater diversity.
Removing hedgerows, monoculture, pesticides and draining wetlands reduce biodiversity. Conservation schemes balance food production with biodiversity.
Compare observable characteristics, base sequences of DNA or mRNA, or amino acid sequences of proteins. More similar sequences show closer relationships.
Use random sampling, large sample sizes and calculate means and standard deviations to compare variation reliably.
Habitat biodiversity, species biodiversity (richness and evenness) and genetic biodiversity.
D = 1 - Σ(n/N)². Values close to 1 mean high diversity; close to 0 mean low diversity.
Random and non-random (opportunistic, stratified, systematic) sampling, using pooters, sweep nets, pitfall traps, kick sampling and quadrats.
Human population growth, agriculture (monoculture), climate change and habitat loss.
Ecological (protecting keystone species), economic (new drugs, soil fertility) and aesthetic reasons.
In situ and ex situ conservation
In situ: protecting species in their natural habitat (marine reserves). Ex situ: outside their habitat (zoos, seed banks, botanic gardens).
CITES regulates trade in endangered species; the Rio Convention on Biological Diversity; the UK Countryside Stewardship Scheme.
The number of different alleles of genes in a population. It allows natural selection to occur.
Random mutation creates new alleles. If an allele gives a selective advantage, those individuals are more likely to survive and reproduce, passing it on, so its frequency increases over generations.
Individuals with an extreme phenotype are favoured, e.g. antibiotic resistance in bacteria.
Individuals with phenotypes near the mean are favoured, reducing variation, e.g. human birth weight.
Anatomical (body structure), physiological (body processes) and behavioural.
Use aseptic technique to spread bacteria on agar, add antibiotic discs and measure clear zones of inhibition; bigger zones show more effective antibiotics.
Prokaryotae, Protoctista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
The evolutionary relationships between organisms, shown in phylogenetic trees.
Palaeontology (fossils), comparative anatomy (homologous structures) and comparative biochemistry (DNA and protein sequences).
Intraspecific and interspecific variation; continuous (shown by histograms, normal distribution) and discontinuous (bar charts).
Standard deviation, Student's t-test and Spearman's rank correlation coefficient.
Pesticides select for resistant insects; resistant alleles become more common.
Maintaining a stable internal environment within limits, which keeps enzymes working optimally and water potential stable.
A change from the norm triggers a response that restores it. Separate mechanisms for increases and decreases give greater control.

Released by β cells in the islets of Langerhans when blood glucose is high. It binds receptors, causes more glucose channels in membranes, and activates enzymes that convert glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis).
Released by α cells when blood glucose is low. Activates glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver.
Adrenaline and glucagon bind receptors, activating adenylate cyclase, which converts ATP to cyclic AMP. cAMP activates protein kinase, which triggers glycogenolysis.
Type I vs type II diabetes
Type I: the body can't produce insulin (autoimmune); treated with insulin injections. Type II: cells don't respond properly to insulin; linked to obesity; treated with diet, exercise and drugs.
Use a calibration curve made from known concentrations of glucose with a colorimeter, or test strips.

Ultrafiltration in the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule; selective reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule; loop of Henle creates a water potential gradient in the medulla; water reabsorbed in the collecting duct.

The ascending limb actively transports Na⁺ out into the medulla and is impermeable to water. This lowers water potential in the medulla, so water leaves the descending limb and collecting duct by osmosis.

When blood water potential falls, osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect it, and the posterior pituitary releases ADH. ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water (more aquaporins), so more water is reabsorbed.
Ectotherms rely on behaviour (basking, burrowing) to control body temperature.
Vasodilation, sweating and lowering body hair to cool; vasoconstriction, shivering and raising hairs to warm. Controlled by the hypothalamus.
Hepatocytes arranged in lobules; blood from the hepatic artery and hepatic portal vein mixes in sinusoids; bile flows to the bile duct.
Storage of glycogen, detoxification of alcohol and drugs, and formation of urea from excess amino acids via the ornithine cycle.
Dialysis (haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis) and kidney transplants.
Pregnancy tests detect hCG using monoclonal antibodies; drug tests detect anabolic steroids.
About -70 mV. Sodium-potassium pumps move 3 Na⁺ out for every 2 K⁺ in, and the membrane is more permeable to K⁺, which diffuses out.
Depolarisation: stimulus opens Na⁺ channels, Na⁺ floods in. Repolarisation: Na⁺ channels close, K⁺ channels open, K⁺ diffuses out. Hyperpolarisation then the resting potential is restored.
If the threshold is reached an action potential always fires with the same size; a bigger stimulus gives more frequent impulses, not bigger ones.
Time when ion channels are recovering and a new action potential can't fire. It makes impulses discrete, one-directional and limits frequency.
Myelination (saltatory conduction between nodes of Ranvier), axon diameter (wider is faster) and temperature.

An action potential opens Ca²⁺ channels in the presynaptic knob; vesicles release acetylcholine by exocytosis; it diffuses across and binds to receptors, opening Na⁺ channels in the postsynaptic membrane.
Hydrolyses acetylcholine in the synaptic cleft, so the response stops and acetylcholine can be recycled.
Spatial: several presynaptic neurones together release enough neurotransmitter. Temporal: one neurone fires rapidly so neurotransmitter builds up to reach threshold.
Neurotransmitters open Cl⁻ channels and K⁺ channels, causing hyperpolarisation, so an action potential is less likely.
Synapse between a motor neurone and a muscle. Always excitatory; only links to muscle; many receptors.
Receptors convert one form of energy into an electrical impulse, e.g. Pacinian corpuscles convert pressure.
Sensory, relay and motor neurones differ in structure and position.
Ductless glands secrete hormones into the blood, which act on target cells with specific receptors.
The cortex secretes steroid hormones (cortisol, aldosterone); the medulla secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline.
Exocrine tissue makes digestive enzymes; endocrine islets of Langerhans contain α cells (glucagon) and β cells (insulin).
High glucose enters β cells and is respired, raising ATP; ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels close, depolarising the cell; Ca²⁺ channels open and insulin is released by exocytosis.
Insulin from genetically modified bacteria and stem cell therapy to replace β cells.
A directional movement towards or away from a stimulus, e.g. woodlice moving away from light.
A non-directional response where the rate of movement or turning changes in response to unfavourable conditions such as humidity.
In shoots, IAA moves to the shaded side and causes cell elongation, so shoots bend towards light. In roots, IAA moves to the lower side and inhibits elongation, so roots bend down (gravitropism).
Receptor, sensory neurone, relay neurone, motor neurone, effector. Fast and involuntary, protecting the body from harm.
A pressure receptor. Pressure deforms the lamellae, opening stretch-mediated sodium channels; sodium ions flow in, creating a generator potential.
Rods are very sensitive (many share one neurone - summation) but give low visual acuity. Cones give colour vision and high acuity, as each has its own neurone, but need bright light.

The SAN sends waves of excitation across the atria; the AVN passes them down the bundle of His and Purkyne tissue. The medulla oblongata alters heart rate via sympathetic (faster) and parasympathetic (slower) nerves.
Found in the aorta and carotid arteries. They detect changes in blood pH (CO2) and blood pressure and send impulses to the medulla.
Made of sarcomeres containing thick myosin and thin actin filaments. The A band contains myosin; the I band contains only actin; the H zone only myosin.

Ca²⁺ ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum bind tropomyosin, moving it so myosin heads bind actin to form cross-bridges. The heads pivot (power stroke), pulling actin past, and ATP detaches them.
ATP hydrolysis provides energy to move and re-cock myosin heads, and to actively transport calcium ions back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum.
Stored in muscle; provides phosphate to regenerate ATP from ADP quickly during short, intense exercise.
Slow-twitch: contract slowly, many mitochondria and myoglobin, for endurance via aerobic respiration. Fast-twitch: contract rapidly, more glycogen and phosphocreatine, for short powerful bursts.
Auxins (cell elongation, apical dominance), gibberellins (stem elongation, seed germination), abscisic acid (stomatal closure), ethene (fruit ripening, leaf abscission).
Auxins in rooting powders and weedkillers; gibberellins in fruit production and brewing; ethene to ripen fruit.
Cerebrum (voluntary actions), cerebellum (balance and coordination), medulla oblongata (heart rate, breathing), hypothalamus (homeostasis) and pituitary gland.
Somatic (voluntary) and autonomic (involuntary) systems; the autonomic is divided into sympathetic and parasympathetic.
The hypothalamus activates the sympathetic nervous system and adrenal medulla, raising heart rate, breathing rate and blood glucose.
Skeletal (striated, voluntary), cardiac (myogenic, branched) and involuntary smooth muscle (in walls of hollow organs).
Simple reflex arcs that protect the body and help maintain balance.
Light energy excites electrons in chlorophyll, which are lost and pass along an electron transfer chain.
Light splits water into protons, electrons and oxygen: 2H2O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O2. Electrons replace those lost from chlorophyll.
Energy from electrons pumps protons into the thylakoid space. Protons diffuse back through ATP synthase, producing ATP. NADP is reduced to reduced NADP.
In the stroma: CO2 combines with ribulose bisphosphate (RuBP), catalysed by rubisco, forming two glycerate 3-phosphate (GP). GP is reduced to triose phosphate (TP) using reduced NADP and ATP.
Five out of every six TP molecules are used to regenerate RuBP using ATP. The rest make glucose and other organic substances.
Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature. Growers manipulate these in glasshouses to maximise yield while staying profitable.
Separate photosynthetic pigments on paper or TLC and calculate Rf values = distance moved by spot ÷ distance moved by solvent.
In isolated chloroplasts, DCPIP (a redox indicator) goes from blue to colourless as it is reduced, showing the rate of the light-dependent reaction.
Non-cyclic uses PSII and PSI, producing ATP, reduced NADP and oxygen. Cyclic uses PSI only, producing only ATP.
The light intensity at which the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration.
In the cytoplasm: glucose is phosphorylated to triose phosphate, which is oxidised to pyruvate. Net gain of 2 ATP and 2 reduced NAD per glucose.
Pyruvate is converted to lactate (animals) or ethanol and CO2 (plants and yeast). This regenerates NAD so glycolysis can continue.
In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate is oxidised to acetate (losing CO2 and producing reduced NAD); acetate combines with coenzyme A to form acetylcoenzyme A.
Acetylcoenzyme A (2C) combines with a 4C molecule to form a 6C molecule. Through oxidation reactions it regenerates the 4C molecule, producing reduced NAD, reduced FAD, ATP and CO2.

Electrons from reduced NAD and FAD pass along the electron transfer chain on the cristae, releasing energy to pump protons into the intermembrane space. Protons flow back through ATP synthase, making ATP.
The final electron acceptor; combines with electrons and protons to form water.
Lipids and proteins can be respired. Glycerol and fatty acids, or amino acids, enter the Krebs cycle.
Measures oxygen uptake. Soda lime absorbs CO2, so movement of the coloured liquid shows oxygen consumed.
RQ = CO2 produced ÷ O2 consumed. Carbohydrates have RQ 1.0, proteins about 0.9 and lipids about 0.7.
Outer and inner membranes, cristae, intermembrane space and matrix, each suited to different stages of respiration.
Addition, deletion, substitution, inversion, duplication and translocation of bases. Addition and deletion cause frameshifts.
Totipotent (can become any cell, early embryo), pluripotent (embryonic stem cells), multipotent (adult stem cells) and unipotent. iPS cells are made from adult cells using transcription factors.
Proteins that move from the cytoplasm into the nucleus and bind to the promoter region of target genes, stimulating or inhibiting transcription.
Oestrogen diffuses into the cell and binds a receptor on a transcription factor, changing its shape so it can bind DNA and start transcription.
Heritable changes in gene function without changes to the base sequence. Increased methylation of DNA and decreased acetylation of histones inhibit transcription.
Small interfering RNA binds to complementary mRNA, which is then broken down, preventing translation.
Benign tumours grow slowly and don't spread; malignant tumours grow rapidly and spread (metastasise).

Mutated proto-oncogenes become oncogenes that are permanently activated. Mutated tumour suppressor genes can no longer slow cell division. Hypermethylation of tumour suppressors and hypomethylation of oncogenes contribute.
High oestrogen levels can activate the transcription of genes that promote cell division, contributing to some breast cancers.

In E. coli, the repressor binds the operator when lactose is absent. Lactose binds the repressor, changing its shape so RNA polymerase can transcribe the genes for β-galactosidase and lactose permease.
Splicing of pre-mRNA removes introns. Post-translational control includes activation of proteins by cAMP.
Highly conserved genes that control body plans. Hox genes control the development of body segments.
Programmed cell death removes unwanted cells, e.g. separating fingers. Stress and stimuli can affect expression of genes controlling development.
Genotype is the genetic makeup; phenotype is the expression of that genetic makeup and its interaction with the environment.
Dominant alleles are always expressed; recessive only when homozygous; codominant alleles are both expressed in the phenotype.
Monohybrid: one gene. Dihybrid: two genes. A typical heterozygous dihybrid cross gives a 9:3:3:1 ratio.
Genes on the X chromosome. Males have only one X, so a single recessive allele is expressed (e.g. haemophilia, colour blindness).
Two genes on the same autosome are inherited together unless crossing over separates them, so fewer recombinant offspring appear than expected.
Genes with more than two alleles, e.g. ABO blood groups, where Iᴬ and Iᴮ are codominant and Iᴼ is recessive.
When the allele of one gene affects or masks the expression of another gene, changing expected ratios.
χ² = Σ(O - E)² ÷ E. Compare to the critical value at p = 0.05 with the right degrees of freedom. If below the critical value, the difference is due to chance.
p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1. Predicts allele frequencies don't change if: large population, no mutation, no migration, random mating and no selection.
Mutation, meiosis (crossing over and independent segregation), random fertilisation and the environment.
Populations are geographically isolated; different selection pressures and mutations change allele frequencies until they can no longer interbreed.
Speciation within the same area due to reproductive isolation, e.g. changes in behaviour, mating season or genitalia.
Random changes in allele frequency, which have the greatest effect in small populations.
A small group starts a new population, or a population is drastically reduced, cutting genetic diversity.
Humans choose individuals with desired traits to breed, e.g. high-yield crops or dairy cattle; reduces genetic diversity.
Sequencing whole genomes. In simple organisms, proteome can be predicted; in complex organisms, non-coding DNA and regulatory genes make this harder.
Reverse transcriptase makes cDNA from mRNA; restriction endonucleases cut DNA at recognition sites, producing sticky ends; or genes can be made with a gene machine.
Insert the gene into a vector (plasmid) using the same restriction enzyme and DNA ligase, transform host cells, and identify them using marker genes.
Heat to 95 °C to separate strands, cool to about 55 °C so primers anneal, heat to 72 °C so DNA polymerase extends. Each cycle doubles the DNA.
Making medicines (e.g. insulin), GM crops (e.g. pest resistance) and gene therapy. Raises ethical, financial and social issues.
Short, labelled single-stranded DNA that binds to complementary sequences, used to screen for alleles linked to disease.
Screening results help people understand risks; drugs and doses can be tailored to a person's genotype.
Uses variable number tandem repeats (VNTRs). DNA is cut, separated by gel electrophoresis and compared. Used in forensics, paternity tests and breeding programmes.
Sanger sequencing uses terminator bases; high-throughput sequencing is fast and automated.
DNA fragments move through a gel towards the positive electrode; smaller fragments travel further.
Somatic cell therapy affects only the treated person; germ line therapy affects future generations and is banned in humans.
Designing and building new biological parts or systems, e.g. producing drugs in microorganisms.
Vegetative propagation produces clones, e.g. runners, bulbs and suckers.
Cuttings and micropropagation by tissue culture. Produces many identical plants quickly but reduces genetic variation.
Artificial embryo twinning (splitting an early embryo) and somatic cell nuclear transfer (as with Dolly the sheep).
Advantages: copies of high-value animals and conservation of rare species. Disadvantages: low success rates, reduced diversity and ethical concerns.
Used for brewing, baking, cheese, yoghurt, penicillin, insulin and bioremediation because they grow fast and in cheap conditions.
Batch culture runs for a set time then stops; continuous culture keeps microbes in the log phase with nutrients added constantly.
Lag, log (exponential), stationary and death phases.
Enzymes fixed in a matrix (e.g. alginate beads) so they can be reused and don't contaminate the product. Used to make lactose-free milk and fructose syrup.
Sterilise equipment, work near a Bunsen flame and keep cultures covered to prevent contamination.
The mass of carbon or dry mass of tissue per given area, measured using calorimetry to find chemical energy stored.
GPP is chemical energy stored in plant biomass. NPP = GPP - R, where R is energy lost in respiration.
N = I - (F + R), where I is chemical energy in ingested food, F is energy lost in faeces and urine, and R is respiratory losses.
Simplifying food webs (pesticides) and reducing respiratory losses (keeping animals warm and still) increase productivity.
Decompose dead matter by extracellular digestion, releasing nutrients back into the soil.
Nitrogen fixation (Rhizobium), ammonification (saprobionts), nitrification (ammonium to nitrites to nitrates by nitrifying bacteria), and denitrification (nitrates to N2 by anaerobic bacteria).
Phosphate ions from rocks are released by weathering, taken up by plants, passed along food chains, released by decomposers and returned to sediments.
Fungal associations with plant roots that increase the surface area for water and mineral uptake.
Natural or artificial fertilisers replace nutrients. Leaching causes eutrophication: algal bloom, light blocked, plants die, decomposers use up oxygen, and fish die.
A population is all organisms of one species in an area. A community is all populations in an area. An ecosystem includes the community and the non-living (abiotic) parts.
The role of a species within its habitat, including biotic and abiotic interactions. Two species can't occupy the same niche indefinitely.
The maximum population size an environment can support, limited by abiotic factors and biotic factors such as competition and predation.
Random quadrats estimate abundance of non-motile organisms; belt or line transects show how species change across a gradient.
Population = (number in first sample × number in second sample) ÷ number marked in second sample. Assumes no migration, births or deaths, and marking doesn't affect survival.
Pioneer species colonise; they change abiotic conditions, making it suitable for other species, increasing biodiversity until a climax community forms.
Managing succession (e.g. grazing or burning) to conserve habitats, balancing conservation with human needs.
Biotic: living factors such as predation and competition. Abiotic: non-living factors such as light, temperature and water.
Usually about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level; the rest is lost through respiration, heat, excretion and uneaten parts.
Populations rise and fall in cycles, with predator numbers lagging behind prey.
Competition between species can exclude one species; competition within a species limits population size.
Coppicing, rotational felling and fishing quotas allow resources to be used without depleting them.
Conflict between conservation and human needs
e.g. the Masai Mara, the Terai region of Nepal and the Peak District balance tourism, farming and wildlife.
